Mathematics as a recorded discipline begins in the fertile valley between the Tigris and Euphrates. The **Sumerians** (c. 3500–2000 BCE) developed one of the earliest writing systems, **cuneiform**, and with it the earliest numerical records. They used a **sexagesimal (base-60)** place-value system, a legacy that survives today in our 60 seconds per minute, 60 minutes per hour, and 360 degrees in a circle.

The most important surviving mathematical artifacts come from **Old Babylonian** period (c. 1900–1600 BCE). Two famous tablets illustrate their sophistication:

**Plimpton 322** (c. 1800 BCE, housed at Columbia University) contains four columns of sexagesimal numbers that appear to list **Pythagorean triples**—sets of integers (a, b, c) satisfying a² + b² = c².
